articles.title: DMARC none quarantine reject: A Safe Rollout Guide
articles.description: DMARC is easy to enable and easy to break. The safe path is not “set p=reject on Friday.” It is a staged rollout: observe first, quarantine the small failures, then reject only when the data is boring. Start at p=none p=none does not enforce anything. It tells receivers to send reports while you learn which senders use your domain. Add a reporting address: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com; fo=1 Wait until you have enough reports to see every legitimate sender. This can take days or weeks depending on volume. Fix alignment before enforcement For each legitimate source, confirm: SPF passes and aligns with the From domain DKIM passes and aligns with the From domain the Return-Path domain is expected third-party senders are authorized A sender can pass SPF but fail DMARC if the domains do not align. Do not confuse “SPF pass” with “DMARC pass.” Move to quarantine Start with a small percentage: v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=10; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com Watch the reports for legitimate mail that fails. Increase pct gradually. Do not jump to 100% just because a test message passed. Reports show the long tail. Move to reject When failures are only from unauthorized or unwanted sources, move to reject: v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com; fo=1 Keep reporting enabled. Reject does not mean you can stop watching. Test the policy before publishing A policy simulator lets you check what would happen to a message under none, quarantine, and reject before changing DNS: https://mailers.email/tools/dmarc-policy-simulator/ Common mistakes enabling reject without reports forgetting a legitimate ESP using a subdomain policy that is stricter than the parent ignoring SPF lookup limits not monitoring the reporting mailbox The rollout rule Observe, fix, quarantine, reject. In that order.
